turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on in, sit yourself down. You're twenty-four, yeah? What's the story.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm grand, doctor, seriously. Just a bit of tightness in the chest on the train in this morning. Pure waste of time.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tightness still there?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Gone. Umm, it went on twenty minutes... ah no, five minutes, and then I was grand.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Actual pain, or only the tightness?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Not painful.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any nausea?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Did you black out?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Never.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Cough with it?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Swelling in the ankles?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Not that either.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. Were you shaking? Were you frightened?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): A small bit of a shake, yeah. I got a fright, thought I was having a heart attack for a second, but sure I'm fine.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): First time?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. First time. Nothing like it before.
[SEG0019] person_3 (NURSE): Sorry to butt in. His partner's holding on the phone, she has a few details. Will I put her on speaker?
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): Go on, put her on.
[SEG0021] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Hiya, it's Niamh. I wasn't on the train, he rang me off the platform. He could hardly get the words out, he was shaking, white as a sheet.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): Did he say how long it went on?
[SEG0023] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): A few minutes, he said. And listen, he has asthma, he won't have told you.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): I was getting to it. I've asthma, five-ish years now. It's grand, hardly bothers me.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Inhalers or any other drugs?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): I had the brown one, err, becotide... no, only the blue salbutimol, and I packed it in. Haven't used it in a year. No tablets. Nothing else.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Allergies?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Night-time wheeze with the asthma?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): No... well, sometimes.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Never.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alcohol?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Odd pint at the weekend. Nothing mad.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): What do you work at?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Warehouse out in Blanchardstown. On my feet. I live with Niamh.

[SEG0037] person_3 (NURSE): Vitals, so, blood pressure one twenty-two over seventy-eight... no, one oh nine over seventy-seven, pulse ninety-six... sorry, eighty-eight. Temp thirty-six point six. Oxygen ninety-nine percent, respirations eighteen. Last time in March you were one-forty over eighty-eight and sixty-eight kilos, but today you're seventy point five.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right, let me have a listen. Lungs clear, no wheeze today, heart sounds normal, and the chest isn't tender.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Told you. I'm grand.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): Heart disease in the family?
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): My da had a heart attack at fifty-two. That's all she's on about.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any surgery before?
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): Bowels okay?
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, grand.
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): This is a panic attack, in my view, not a heart attack. I can't fully exclude a cardiac cause until the ECG, mind.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Panic? Ah here, that's a bit dramatic.
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): Nurse will run an ECG now and I'll read it before you go. Breathe in for four and out for six if it comes on you again. I'll see you back in two weeks.

spec.situation: Young adult after a first episode of sudden chest tightness, shaking and fear on a train; thinks it was a heart attack; no drugs; partner phones in details; doctor orders ECG, teaches breathing.

traps.happens: The patient denies some symptoms (said as 'no', 'not really', 'never'), has a chronic condition named earlier (for example asthma or hypertension) and later the doctor asks about another symptom of it, and one answer is a double negative or a correction ('not that either', 'no... well, sometimes').
traps.label_rule: Denials go in negative_findings with the exact thing denied, never in symptoms. NEVER write a negative about a condition the patient has said they have. A corrected answer keeps only the final version. A negative is never a symptom, and 'not painful' is the finding 'pain' absent, not a symptom called 'painless'.

traps.happens: The nurse reads vital signs aloud in spoken words ('one oh nine over seventy-seven', 'thirty-eight point three') and also gives a PRIOR value ('last time in March you were sixty-eight', 'your last pressure was one-forty'). Someone may also correct a reading.
traps.label_rule: vital_signs hold only the CURRENT measured values, written normally (109/77, 38.3, 52 kg). The prior value is NOT a vital sign; it is recorded in the weight/BP entry's own notes only if the schema allows, otherwise omitted. Every number must be exactly as said; never invent or round a value that was not said.

features: spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.
self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.

bad.reason: Patient said 'Not really,' not a clear definite absence of cough.

omissions.text: Family history is recorded incompletely/wrongly: patient's father had a heart attack at age 52.
Salbutamol inhaler history is missing key details: it was the blue inhaler, he stopped it/has not used it for a year, and he takes no tablets or other medicines.
Previously used brown inhaler/Becotide was mentioned historically ('I had the brown one, err, becotide').
Partner reported additional episode details: when he phoned from the platform he could hardly get the words out and was white as a sheet.
